title: Implant Internal Image
summary: Implant Internal Image is persistence that lives in the templates an organisation uses to build workloads. Cloud providers distribute machine images, containers start from base images, and internal registries hold the approved versions of both. An adversary who already holds credentials in that environment can push a modified image, or overwrite an existing tag, so that any instance, virtual machine, or container created from it later already contains the code of the attacker. The dependency on automation is what makes it durable: provisioning pipelines and orchestrators that always deploy the newest or floating tag will keep recreating the backdoor without any further attacker action, and the routine image refresh process can even make the compromise look like a normal update to a clean system. This differs from uploading malware to a public repository, because the implanted image sits inside the registry of the victim and is trusted by their build and deploy tooling. Detection leans on registry and audit records: image push and tag retarget events, unexpected digests for an image tag, publishers or pipelines that have never pushed that repository before, and new layers, files, or entrypoint changes in the image. Forensic confirmation usually comes from inspecting the deployed instance itself for files and processes that are absent from the approved build.

beginner.definition: A machine image is a ready-made copy of a computer or an application that new servers are created from. This technique is about an attacker hiding harmful code inside one of those copies, inside your own cloud or container storage. Every new server built from that copy then starts with the code of the attacker already inside it.
beginner.whyItMatters: This kind of persistence is very hard to notice, because the harmful code arrives with a legitimate deployment. You can rebuild a server or delete a container and the problem comes straight back the next time the pipeline runs. It also gives the attacker access to everything the new workload can reach, including databases and internal networks. Standard malware scanning of one running server will not tell you that the source image is poisoned.
howItWorks: The attacker first gets cloud credentials or access to a build environment.
They find where images and containers are stored, such as a registry or image catalogue.
They download an approved image and add their own code, often a small remote access script.
They publish the modified image, sometimes replacing the tag that teams already use.
The build or provisioning system creates new servers from the newest image automatically.
Each new server starts with the hidden code, and the attacker returns to it later.
beginner.example: Imagine an office kitchen where every new worker bakes a cake from the same printed recipe card on the wall. Someone quietly edits the card to add a secret ingredient. Nobody watches the oven closely, the cakes still look and taste normal, and every cake baked from that day onward contains it.
takeaways: Trusted images are a source of code, so their changes matter as much as source code changes.
Watch who pushes images and whether an existing tag suddenly points to a new version.
A clean server is not proof of a clean image underneath it.

objectives: Explain how image and container registries can carry persistence into new workloads.
Describe how provisioning pipelines recreate an implanted image automatically.
Identify registry audit events that reveal unexpected image pushes or tag changes.
Compare an implanted image against the approved build baseline.
Recommend signing, scanning and tag policies that reduce this risk.
